sub: Many English sayings are ancient — some come straight from Latin. Read the clues, trace them across languages, and separate the saying from its meaning.
kw: proverbs sayings latin carpe diem seize the day the apple doesn't fall far from the tree de tal palo tal astilla better late than never más vale tarde early bird etymology roots english spanish latin figurative language multilingual world languages high school grade 9 10 11 12

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Trace sayings to their meaning and their roots
brief.p: A proverb is a short, traditional saying that carries a lesson. Some English sayings even come from Latin. Find the meaning, compare it across languages, and notice where it came from.

win.p: You matched proverbs to their meanings, compared them across languages, and traced a Latin root — sophisticated work with figurative and traditional language.

clues.title: 'The apple doesn't fall far from the tree'
clues.body: This proverb means children resemble their parents. Spanish says 'de tal palo, tal astilla' (from such a stick, such a splinter) — a different picture, the same lesson.

clues.title: 'Better late than never'
clues.body: 'Better late than never' means doing something late is better than not at all. Spanish says 'más vale tarde que nunca' — an almost exact match, phrase for phrase.

clues.title: A Latin saying inside English
clues.body: 'Carpe diem' is a Latin phrase used in English that means 'seize the day' — make the most of now. Because Spanish also descends from Latin, it shares the root: Spanish 'día' (day) comes from Latin 'diem.'

clues.title: 'The early bird catches the worm'
clues.body: This means those who act early get the reward. Spanish has a vivid saying about the same idea of not being lazy: 'camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente' (a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried off by the current) — a completely different picture, a related lesson.

clues.title: Two kinds of figurative language
clues.body: A quick distinction: an IDIOM is a fixed figurative phrase ('spill the beans'). A PROVERB is a short, traditional saying that states a general LESSON about life ('the early bird catches the worm'). Both are figurative — but a proverb teaches, while an idiom just names.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: One of the longest ancient scrolls ever found is over 40 meters long. That is a true history fact — but it has nothing to do with what these sayings mean.

locks.title: Tell the genres apart
locks.q: What makes a PROVERB different from an ordinary idiom?
options: A proverb states a general life lesson; an idiom is just a fixed figurative phrase
A proverb is always longer than an idiom
A proverb must come from Latin
locks.reason: A proverb teaches a general lesson ('better late than never'); an idiom is simply a fixed figurative expression ('spill the beans'). Length and Latin origin don't define a proverb — its job of teaching a lesson does.

locks.title: Which claims hold up?
locks.q: Check every TRUE statement. One makes a false claim about where languages and proverbs come from — leave it out.

items.t: A proverb is a short, traditional saying that carries a general lesson
Some sayings, like 'carpe diem,' entered English directly from Latin
The Latin word 'diem' is the root of the Spanish word 'día'
Since English and Spanish both come from Latin, their proverbs are usually identical

locks.reason: The false statement is doubly wrong: English is mainly Germanic (not descended from Latin), and even related languages usually express a proverb with a DIFFERENT image ('de tal palo, tal astilla' vs. 'the apple doesn't fall far from the tree').

locks.title: Build the lesson
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that explains 'the early bird catches the worm.'

pads.e: 🐛 'So she gets the best chances first.'

locks.reason: The order builds the lesson: acting early, getting the first chances, and the proverb that names it. Proverbs compress a whole lesson into a single line.

locks.title: Trace it back to Latin
locks.q: You've traced 'carpe diem' → Spanish 'día' (day). Type the ORIGINAL Latin word — the one inside 'carpe diem' — that this whole chain started from.
locks.reason: Latin 'diem' (day) is the root that survives in Spanish 'día.' Tracing a modern word BACK to its Latin source — not just forward — is core etymology work for advanced and Latin students.

h1: Wild Goose Chase: Idioms from Literature
sub: Many everyday idioms were coined by writers centuries ago. Trace them to their literary source, compare across languages, and crack the escalating locks.
kw: idioms literature shakespeare othello allusion wild goose chase green-eyed monster in a pickle etymology origin english spanish figurative language multilingual world languages high school grade 9 10 11 12

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Trace idioms to their literary roots
brief.p: Some idioms you use every day were invented by writers — Shakespeare especially. Find the meaning, notice the allusion, and compare across languages.

win.p: You matched idioms to meanings, spotted their literary origins, and reasoned about language. Sophisticated allusion and etymology work.

clues.title: 'A wild goose chase'
clues.body: A 'wild goose chase' is a hopeless, pointless pursuit. Shakespeare used it in Romeo and Juliet (~1595). Spanish says 'una búsqueda inútil' (a useless search) — no goose.

clues.title: 'The green-eyed monster'
clues.body: The 'green-eyed monster' means jealousy. Shakespeare coined it in Othello. Spanish says 'el monstruo de los celos' (the monster of jealousy) — a close match.

clues.title: 'In a pickle'
clues.body: To be 'in a pickle' means to be in a difficult spot. Shakespeare used it in The Tempest. Spanish says 'estar en un aprieto' (to be in a tight spot) — a different picture.

clues.title: Where idioms come from
clues.body: Hundreds of English idioms first appeared in literature and were repeated until they became everyday phrases. Shakespeare alone gave English dozens of them.

clues.title: Idioms are allusions
clues.body: When a phrase points back to an older text — a play, a myth, the Bible studied as literature — that's an allusion. Idioms are allusions we've stopped noticing.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Writers of Shakespeare's era wrote with quill pens cut from goose feathers. That's a true history fact — but not what these idioms mean.

locks.title: Name it and its source
locks.q: Which idiom names JEALOUSY, and which writer coined it?
options: 'the green-eyed monster,' coined by Shakespeare in Othello
'wild goose chase,' from a hunting manual
locks.reason: Clue 2: Shakespeare coined 'the green-eyed monster' for jealousy in Othello. Recognizing an idiom's literary source is an allusion skill.

locks.title: Which claims hold up?
locks.q: Check every TRUE statement. One overgeneralizes — leave it out.

items.t: An idiom can be an allusion to an older text we've stopped noticing
Shakespeare coined many idioms still used in everyday English
'Green-eyed monster' (English) and 'monstruo de los celos' (Spanish) both name jealousy
Every English idiom was invented by Shakespeare

locks.reason: The false statement overgeneralizes: Shakespeare coined MANY, but idioms also come from the Bible-as-literature, myth, sailing, sports, and daily life.

locks.title: Follow two idioms
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes sense — using BOTH 'wild goose chase' and 'in a pickle.'

pads.e: 🪿 'The whole trip was a wild goose chase.'
🗺️ 'We drove for hours to the wrong address.'
🥒 'Now we're in a pickle — we're late.'

locks.reason: The order builds a story: a fruitless search ('wild goose chase') that leaves them in trouble ('in a pickle'). Tracking two literary idioms across a passage is real reading.

locks.title: Name the source
locks.q: Many of the idioms you use every day were first written by one playwright about 400 years ago. Type his last name.
locks.reason: Shakespeare coined 'wild goose chase,' 'the green-eyed monster,' 'in a pickle,' and dozens more. Tracing everyday idioms back to a single literary source is advanced allusion work.

h1: Register & Tone: When to Use an Idiom
sub: Idioms are colorful — but not for every occasion. Learn when an idiom fits and when it doesn't, compare across languages, and crack the escalating locks.
kw: idioms register formal informal tone audience slang appropriate essay english spanish figurative language pragmatics multilingual world languages high school grade 9 10 11 12

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Match the idiom to the moment
brief.p: Idioms are usually informal. Knowing WHEN to use one — and when to choose plain, formal language — is an advanced skill. Read for register, and compare across languages.

win.p: You judged when an idiom fits, compared register across languages, and reasoned about tone. That's pragmatic, advanced language use.

clues.title: Idioms are usually casual
clues.body: Most idioms are INFORMAL — perfect for talking with friends ('hit the books,' 'a piece of cake'), but risky in a formal essay or job application.

clues.title: What 'register' means
clues.body: 'Register' means how formal your language is. You match your register to your audience and purpose: casual with friends, formal in an interview or an academic paper.

clues.title: When an idiom doesn't fit
clues.body: In a formal essay, an idiom can sound out of place. 'The economy went belly-up' is too casual; 'the economy collapsed' fits a formal register.

clues.title: Not just English
clues.body: Register exists in every language. Spanish marks it with 'tú' (informal) vs. 'usted' (formal), and with casual vs. formal wording. Choosing the right level is part of knowing a language well.

clues.title: Idioms set a tone
clues.body: Idioms also set a TONE — playful, blunt, warm. The same idea can sound friendly ('give it a shot') or formal ('make an attempt'). You choose based on the effect you want.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Standard printer paper is about 0.1 mm thick, and A4 is the world's most common size. That's a true fact — but not what register means.

locks.title: Match the register
locks.q: You're writing a FORMAL scholarship essay. Which sentence fits the register?
options: 'I worked hard to reach my goals.'
'I really hit the books to reach my goals.'
'Reaching my goals was a piece of cake.'
locks.reason: A formal essay calls for plain, formal language. The idioms ('hit the books,' 'a piece of cake') are too casual for that audience — matching register to purpose is the skill.

locks.title: Which claims hold up?
locks.q: Check every TRUE statement about register. Leave out the false one.

items.t: Most idioms belong to an informal register
You choose your register to fit your audience and purpose
Register exists in other languages too (Spanish 'tú' vs. 'usted')
Idioms are appropriate in every situation, including formal writing

locks.reason: The false statement ignores register: idioms usually don't fit formal writing. Knowing WHEN to use one is the whole point.

locks.title: Order the decision
locks.q: Tap the three steps in the ORDER you'd use to decide whether to use an idiom.

pads.e: 🎚️ 'That tells me my register — casual or formal.'
🎯 'First: who is my audience, and what's my purpose?'
✅ 'Then I choose — an idiom, or plain formal words.'

locks.reason: The order is the decision process: audience & purpose → register → word choice. Making register a conscious step is advanced, pragmatic language use.

locks.title: Name the register
locks.q: Idioms usually belong to which register — formal or informal? Type it (one word).
locks.reason: Idioms are usually INFORMAL. Naming their default register — and knowing to swap in plain language when formality is required — is a sophisticated pragmatic skill.

h1: French Idioms: The Same Idea in Another Language
sub: French is full of idioms too — ropes for rain, cake for easy, a rabbit for standing someone up. Read the clues, compare French to English, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms french france lote world language classical c'est du gâteau il pleut des cordes poser un lapin donner sa langue au chat coûter les yeux cross-linguistic figurative language high school grade 9 10 11 12

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: An idiom's meaning is never the sum of its words — in any language. Compare each French idiom's picture to English: sometimes the same (cake), sometimes different (ropes vs. cats), sometimes with no parallel at all. That comparison is the heart of learning a language.

win.p: You compared French and English idioms — matching images, contrasting images, and idioms unique to one culture. That cross-linguistic eye is exactly what strong world-language learners build.

clues.title: 'C'est du gâteau' (it's cake)
clues.body: 'C'est du gâteau' means something is very easy. English says 'a piece of cake' — the SAME picture: cake. When two languages share the image, the idiom is easy to remember.

clues.title: 'Il pleut des cordes' (it's raining ropes)
clues.body: 'Il pleut des cordes' means it is raining very hard. English says 'raining cats and dogs' — a DIFFERENT picture (ropes vs. animals), but the very same rainstorm.

clues.title: 'Poser un lapin' (to place a rabbit)
clues.body: 'Poser un lapin à quelqu'un' means to stand someone up — to not show up when you agreed to meet. There is no clean English idiom for it: a saying unique to French.

clues.title: 'Donner sa langue au chat' (give your tongue to the cat)
clues.body: 'Donner sa langue au chat' means to give up trying to guess an answer. English has no matching idiom — another French-only picture worth studying.

clues.title: How idioms travel between languages
clues.body: French idioms, like English ones, do not add up word-for-word. Compare the images: sometimes the same (cake), sometimes different (ropes vs. cats), sometimes with no parallel at all. Noticing which is which makes you a language detective.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The Eiffel Tower in Paris stands about 330 meters tall. That is a true fact about France — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: In French, 'poser un lapin à quelqu'un' really means…
options: to fail to show up for a meeting — to stand someone up
to give someone a pet rabbit
to move quietly, like a rabbit
locks.reason: Clue 3 says it means to stand someone up. The literal picture — placing a rabbit — is the trap. Idioms almost never mean what the words literally say, in French or English.

locks.title: What is true about idioms across languages?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the one that is false.

items.t: French idioms, like English ones, are not the sum of their words
French 'c'est du gâteau' and English 'a piece of cake' use the same picture — cake
'Il pleut des cordes' and 'raining cats and dogs' paint the same rainstorm with different pictures
You can always translate a French idiom word-for-word into English and keep the meaning

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: word-for-word translation is exactly what breaks idioms. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the story in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes 'poser un lapin' make sense.

pads.e: 🕕 'We agreed to meet at the café at six.'
😞 'I waited a whole hour, but she never came.'
😠 'Elle t'a posé un lapin — she stood you up!'

locks.reason: The context reveals the meaning: a plan is made, one person waits, no one comes — that no-show is what 'poser un lapin' names. Idioms depend on context.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: In English, an easy task is 'a piece of ___.' In French, 'c'est du ___' — the SAME food. Type that food in English OR French.
locks.reason: Both languages use cake: English 'cake,' French 'gâteau.' When the picture matches across languages, it helps you remember the idiom.

h1: Latin Roots & Sayings: Where Our Words Come From
sub: Latin is the seedbed of English, Spanish, and French. Meet famous Latin sayings — and watch one root, tempus, grow into 'time,' 'tiempo,' and 'temps.' Compare the languages and crack the locks.
kw: latin proverbs roots etymology classical languages lote subchapter d tempus fugit festina lente veni vidi vici ad astra per aspera romance languages spanish french italian time flies motto high school grade 9 10 11 12

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Trace Latin sayings and roots across languages
brief.p: Many English and Romance-language sayings grew from Latin. Read each Latin saying, find what it really means, and follow its roots into Spanish, French, and English. Etymology turns a hard word into a familiar friend.

win.p: You traced Latin sayings and roots into English, Spanish, and French. Seeing the shared root beneath many languages is exactly how classical-language scholars read the world.

clues.title: 'Tempus fugit' (time flees)
clues.body: 'Tempus fugit' means time flies. English 'time flies,' Spanish 'el tiempo vuela,' and French 'le temps file' all carry the same idea — and Latin 'tempus' is the shared root behind 'time,' 'tiempo,' 'temps,' and 'temporal.'

clues.title: 'Festina lente' (make haste slowly)
clues.body: 'Festina lente' advises you to hurry carefully — go steadily so you don't wreck the job by rushing. English says 'more haste, less speed' and 'slow and steady wins the race': different words, the same wisdom.

clues.title: 'Ad astra per aspera' (to the stars through hardships)
clues.body: 'Ad astra per aspera' means you reach great things by pushing through difficulty. It is still used today as a motto — for example, by the U.S. state of Kansas.

clues.title: 'Veni, vidi, vici' (I came, I saw, I conquered)
clues.body: Reportedly said by Julius Caesar after a fast victory, 'veni, vidi, vici' means a swift, complete success. Three short words in a deliberate order became one of history's most famous sayings.

clues.title: Latin is a seedbed
clues.body: Latin's sayings and roots grew into English, Spanish, French, and Italian. Spotting the root — 'tempus' inside 'time,' 'tiempo,' 'temps,' 'temporal' — turns a hard word into a familiar one. That makes you an etymology detective.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The Roman Colosseum could hold roughly 50,000 spectators. That is a true fact about ancient Rome — but it has nothing to do with what these Latin sayings mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: 'Festina lente' ('make haste slowly') really advises you to…
options: work quickly but carefully — don't rush into mistakes
run as fast as you possibly can
locks.reason: Clue 2 explains that 'festina lente' means hurry carefully. It is not 'go as fast as possible' and not 'always be slow' — it is the balance between them, like 'slow and steady wins the race.'

locks.title: What is true about Latin roots?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the one that is false.

items.t: Latin 'tempus' is the root behind English 'temporal,' Spanish 'tiempo,' and French 'temps'
'Veni, vidi, vici' means 'I came, I saw, I conquered'
Latin sayings and roots grew into English and the Romance languages
Latin is a dead language, so its words never appear in modern English

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: Latin roots are alive in thousands of English and Romance-language words. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put Caesar's saying in order
locks.q: Tap the three Latin words in the ORDER that matches the meaning 'I came, I saw, I conquered.'
locks.reason: The power of the saying is its order: arrival, then observation, then victory — each following fast on the last. Change the order and the story of a swift conquest falls apart.

locks.title: Follow the root across languages
locks.q: Latin 'tempus' means time. It grew into Spanish 'tiempo' and French 'temps.' Type the modern word for 'time' in Spanish OR French.
locks.reason: Latin 'tempus' → Spanish 'tiempo,' French 'temps,' and English words like 'temporal' and 'tempo.' One Latin root, living in many languages at once.
